big: Four objections turn up in almost every client meeting this year: rates, gold, fixed deposits and market highs. Each has a short honest answer, and each answer has a number behind it.

lines: The RBI raised rates in October. Gold beat my equity. My FD pays 7%. And the market is at a high. Should I just stop my SIPs?
Four worries, four calculations. Let us answer each with arithmetic, not with comfort.

h: What a rate rise does to debt funds
alt: Bars comparing the price fall and the months of interest needed to recover it for a short-duration and a long-duration fund
caps: On 7 October 2026 the RBI raised the repo rate by 0.25 point to 5.50%. Bond prices fall when yields rise.
Assume yields rise 0.25 point. A duration-2 fund loses about 0.5%. A duration-6 fund loses about 1.5%.
At an assumed 7% yield, that is under a month of interest for the short fund, and 2.6 months for the long one.
A rate rise hits debt funds by duration. It is no reason to stop a ten-year equity SIP.

h: ₹1 lakh in a 7% FD for 10 years
alt: Four bars showing the FD value before tax, after tax, and after inflation in thousands of rupees
caps: ₹1 lakh in a 7% FD grows to about ₹1.97 lakh in ten years, before tax. Bars are in ₹ thousand.
For a client in the 30% slab (31.2% with cess), interest is taxed every year. About ₹1.60 lakh is left.
If inflation averages an assumed 5%, that ₹1.60 lakh buys what ₹98,000 buys today.
The FD has stood still in real terms. That is the number to compare, not 7%.

alt: Three bars showing a portfolio plan, the mix after gold rises, and the mix after rebalancing
caps: A ₹10 lakh plan: 50% equity, 35% debt, 15% gold. In a year gold gains 40%, equity 2%, debt 7% (made up).
Gold is now 19% of ₹10.95 lakh. The plan said 15%.
Rebalance: sell about ₹46,000 of gold and add it to equity and debt. Back to the plan.
You sell what ran and buy what lagged. That is discipline, not chasing.

q: The RBI raised the repo rate last month. A client with a ₹25,000 equity SIP and a debt fund of duration 6 says: stop the SIP and get out of debt. What do you advise?
opts: Stop the SIP, since equity falls whenever rates rise
Move all his money into a long-duration gilt fund now
Stop the SIP and the debt fund and wait in savings
Keep the SIP; check the debt fund's duration fit
why: Rates can move markets for a while, but a ten-year SIP buys through such phases. Stopping reacts to one event with a long plan.
Long duration is the most exposed to a further rise. Switching into it after a hike adds the very risk he is worried about.
Waiting in savings makes two timing calls at once and earns little. A 0.25-point rise costs a duration-6 fund about 1.5% once.
The equity SIP has a long goal, and the debt fund's hit is small and recoverable. Check whether its duration fits his horizon.

q: In a ₹10 lakh plan of 50% equity, 35% debt and 15% gold, gold gains 40%, equity 2% and debt 7% in a year. The client wants to sell equity and buy more gold. What do you say?
opts: Sell about ₹46,000 of gold, add it to equity and debt
Sell equity and buy more gold, since gold is the leader
Sell all the gold, since it has clearly run too far
Do nothing, since weights need not be reset every year
why: Gold is ₹2.10 lakh of ₹10.945 lakh, 19.2%. Back to 15% means about ₹1.64 lakh, so sell about ₹46,000 and restock the rest.
That chases last year's winner at a higher price, and sells equity that lagged. It breaks the plan the client agreed to follow.
Selling all the gold overshoots. The plan wants 15% in gold, so only the excess above that weight needs trimming.
Left alone, the weights drift to whatever ran most, so risk drifts too. A periodic reset keeps the plan's risk as agreed.

q: A client in the 30% tax slab asks why he should take equity risk when his FD pays 7%. What is the most honest reply?
opts: Equity always beats 7%, so the FD is simply a mistake
FD interest escapes tax, so the 7% reaches him in full
FD for near goals; its real return is about zero
Equity cannot lose money over seven years, so skip the FD
why: Equity has no guarantee. It may beat the FD over long periods or may not, and a promise would be misselling.
FD interest is added to income and taxed at his slab. That is why 7% shrinks to about 4.8% for him.
At 31.2% tax the 7% becomes about 4.8%, near an assumed 5% inflation. The FD is safe and fits near goals, but does not grow wealth.
Equity can fall hard over seven years. Saying otherwise implies an assured outcome, which breaks the compliance rules.

q: A client has ₹30 lakh from a property sale and will not invest because the Nifty is at an all-time high. He wants to wait for a 10% fall. What is the better approach?
opts: Wait; every high is followed by a fall of at least 10%
Hold it safely and STP it in over 6 to 12 months
Invest it all today, since waiting has never paid
Put it all in gold until the market becomes cheaper
why: Markets at highs can keep rising for years. A rule that a 10% fall must follow is a guess, and waiting has its own cost.
Staged entry spreads the timing risk, so he is not betting on one day, and he can stay with the plan whichever way it goes.
Never paid is also false: a lump sum placed just before a fall hurts. His fear of regret is a real input into the plan.
Gold is its own risky asset and can fall too. Swapping one timing bet for another is not a plan.

pts: A rate rise hits debt funds by duration, about 0.25% for each year of duration per 0.25-point rise. It is no reason to stop an equity SIP.
Rebalance to targets: sell what ran, buy what lagged. Do not chase last year's winner.
An FD at 7% in the 30% slab earns about 4.8% after tax, near inflation. For market highs, use SIP or STP.
